params.name: c
params.resample_while: c == 0 or c == P or c == -P

stem: The graph of $g(x) = -{=a}\cdot {=b}^x + q$ passes through the point $({=x0}, {=c})$. Which of the following is the range of $g$?
solution: The point $({=x0}, {=c})$ is on the graph, so substitute $x = {=x0}$ and $g(x) = {=c}$ into $g(x) = -{=a}\cdot {=b}^x + q$: ${=c} = -{=a}\cdot {=b}^{{=x0}} + q$.
Now $a = -{=a}$ is negative and $q = {=q}$. Since $a < 0$, $-{=a}\cdot {=b}^x$ is negative for every $x$, so $g(x) < {=q}$: the graph lies below the line $y = {=q}$.
The graph never reaches $y = {=q}$, so the range is $y \in (-\infty, {=q})$, with a round bracket.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Takes the y-coordinate of the given point as q
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student treats the y-value of the point on the graph as the value of q, forgetting that for y = ab^x + q the value of the function at that point is made up of ab^x as well as q.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Subtracts instead of adding when solving for q
proposed_misconceptions.description: From c = -P + q the student writes q = c - P instead of q = c + P, moving the term across the equals sign without changing its sign.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Ignores the sign of a
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student finds q correctly but says the range lies above y = q even though a is negative, so the graph lies below it.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Includes y = q in the range
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student writes a square bracket, [q, infinity) or (-infinity, q], as if the graph reached the line y = q. It only gets closer and closer, so the bracket must be round.

notes: Advanced tier, modelled on the book's 50(f), where q of g is not given but found from a point on the graph before the range is read. Here the point is on g itself, with x0 = 1 or 2 so q needs a power and a coefficient, then the sign of a decides the side of y = q. q is never 0 (c != -P) and c != 0, c != P keep all five options distinct. a is always negative in this family; the positive direction is a distractor. mcq because the answer is an interval with infinity: all distractors are named, specific slips.
